coal.e: From Middle English col, from Old English col, from Proto-West Germanic *kol, from Proto-Germanic *kulą (“coal”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵwelH- (“to burn, shine”).
coal.g: A black or brownish black rock formed from prehistoric plant remains, composed largely of carbon and burned as a fuel.

coast.e: From Middle English coste (“rib; side of the body”), from Old French coste (“rib; side of an object; coast”) (modern French côte (“rib; coast; hill, slope”)), from Latin costa (“rib; side, wall”).
coast.g: The edge of the land where it meets an ocean, sea, gulf, bay, or large lake.

coast.e: From Middle English costeien (“to travel along a border or coast; to go alongside (something), skirt; to accompany, follow; to travel across, traverse; to be adjacent to, to border;”), from Anglo-Norman, Old French costoier (“to be at the side of”) (modern French côtoyer (“to pass alongside; (figuratively) to rub shoulders”)), from Latin costicāre.
coast.g: To glide along without adding energy; to allow a vehicle to continue moving forward after disengaging the engine or ceasing to apply motive

coastline.g: The shape, outline, or boundary of a coast. (The term coastline is generally used to describe the approximate boundaries at relatively large

coat.e: From Middle English cote, coate, cotte, from Old French cote, cotte (“outer garment with sleeves”), from Latin cotta (“undercoat, tunic”), from Proto-Germanic *kuttô, *kuttǭ (“cowl, woolen cloth, coat”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷewd-, *gud- (“woolen clothes”).
coat.g: An outer garment covering the upper torso and arms.

cobra.e: Borrowed from Portuguese cobra, from Latin colubra (“a female snake”).
cobra.g: Any of the genus Naja of venomous snakes that can spread their neck ribs into a broad hood when threatened; a true cobra.

cobweb.e: From Middle English copweb, coppeweb, coppewebbe, from Old English ātorcoppe (“spider”) + Old English webb. By surface analysis, cob (“spider”, obsolete) + web.
cobweb.g: A spiderweb, especially a large one, an old abandoned one covered with debris and dust or an asymmetrical one woven with an irregular patter

cock.e: From Middle English cok, from Old English coc, cocc (“cock, male bird”), from Proto-West Germanic *kokk, from Proto-Germanic *kukkaz (“cock”), probably of onomatopoeic origin. Reinforced by Old French coc, from the same origin. The sense "penis" is attested since at least the 1610s, with the compound pillicock (“penis”) attested since 1325.

From Middle English cokke, cock, cok, from Old English *cocc (“heap, pile”, attested in place names), from Proto-West Germanic *kokk, from Proto-Germanic *kukkaz (“mass, bulge, swelling”), from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to bend, curve, arch”).
cock.g: A small conical pile of hay or grass.

cockatrice.e: From Middle English cocatrice, from Old French cocatriz (“basilisk, cockatrice”), from Late Latin calcātrīx (“female trampler, treader”), from Latin calcāre (“to trample, to walk upon, to oppress”) + -trīx (“-ess: forming feminine agentives”), from calx (“heel”). Its eventual association with poultry influenced by cock (“rooster, male chicken”), q.v.
cockatrice.g: Synonym of basilisk, a serpentine dragon so poisonous that even its gaze is deadly.

cockcrowing.e: From Middle English cok crowynge; equivalent to cock + crowing.
cockcrowing.g: The crowing sound of a cock.

cockle.e: From Middle English cokel, cokkel, kokkel, cocle, of uncertain origin. Perhaps a diminutive of Middle English cokke, cok (“cockle”), from Old English cocc (found in sǣcocc (“cockle”)) + -le; or perhaps from Old French coquille, from Vulgar Latin *cocchilia, from conchylia.
cockle.g: Any of various edible European bivalve mollusks, of the family Cardiidae, having heart-shaped shells.

cockle.e: From Middle English cockil, cokil, cokylle, from Old English coccel (“darnel”), of unknown origin, perhaps from a diminutive of Latin coccus (“berry”).
cockle.g: Any of several field weeds, such as the common corncockle (Agrostemma githago) and darnel ryegrass (Lolium temulentum).

cocoon.e: From French cocon, a diminutive of coque (“shell”).
cocoon.g: The silky case spun by the larvae of some insects in which they metamorphose, protecting the pupa within.

code.e: From Middle English code (“system of law”), from Old French code (“system of law”), from Latin cōdex, later form of caudex (“the stock or stem of a tree, a board or tablet of wood smeared over with wax, on which the ancients originally wrote; hence, a book, a writing.”). Verb etymology 1, verb sense 7 is an ellipsis of code blue (“medical emergency”).
code.g: A short textual designation, often with little relation to the item it represents.

coexist.g: To exist contemporaneously or in the same area.

coffer.e: From Middle English cofre, coffre, from Old French cofre, coffre, from Latin cophinus (“basket”), from Ancient Greek κόφινος (kóphinos, “basket”).
coffer.g: A strong chest or box used for keeping money or valuables safe.

coffin.e: From Middle English coffyn, from Old Northern French cofin (“sarcophagus", earlier "basket, coffer”), from Latin cophinus (“basket”), a loanword from Ancient Greek κόφινος (kóphinos, “a basket”).
coffin.g: A closed box in which the body of a dead person is placed for burial.

coffin.e: Borrowed from Cornish koghyn (“exploratory mining trench”), with spelling likely influenced by etymology 1.
coffin.g: An exploratory trench used when first digging a mine.

cogitation.e: Latinism, likely a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin cogitatio, cogitationis, possibly influenced by or displacing an earlier doublet of cogitacion inherited from Middle English cogitacioun, from an Old French cogitaciun, from Vulgar Latin cōgitātiō, cōgitātiōnem; compare Middle French cogitatiun, French cogitation.
cogitation.g: The process of cogitating; contemplation, deliberation, reflection, meditation.

coherent.e: From Middle French coherent, from Latin cohaērēns, from co- + haereō. By surface analysis, cohere + -ent.
coherent.g: Unified; sticking together; making up a whole.

coil.e: From Middle English coilen, from Old French coillir, cuillir (“to gather, pluck, pick, cull”) (modern French cueillir), from Latin colligō (“to gather together”), past participle collectus, from com- (“together”) + legō (“to gather”); compare legend.
coil.g: Something wound in the form of a helix or spiral.

coin.e: From Middle English coyn, from Old French coigne (“wedge, cornerstone, die for stamping”), from Latin cuneus (“wedge”).
coin.g: A piece of currency, usually metallic and in the shape of a disc, but sometimes polygonal, or with a hole in the middle.

cold.e: From Middle English cold, from Anglian Old English cald. The West Saxon form, ċeald (“cold”), survived as early Middle English cheald, cheld, or chald. Both descended from Proto-West Germanic *kald, from Proto-Germanic *kaldaz (“cold”), a participle form of *kalaną (“to be cold, to freeze”), from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to be cold, to freeze”).
From Middle English cold, colde, from Old English cald, ċeald (“cold, coldness”), from Proto-West Germanic *kald, from Proto-Germanic *kaldą (“coldness”), from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”).

collapse.e: From Latin collāpsus (past participle of collābor).
collapse.g: To break apart and fall down suddenly; to cave in.

collar.e: From Middle English coler, borrowed from Old French coler (Modern French collier), from Late Latin collāre, from Latin collāris, from collum (“neck”).

collateral.e: Recorded since c.1378, from Old French, from Medieval Latin collaterālis, from Latin col- (“together with”) (a form of con-) + the stem of latus (“side”). By surface analysis, col- + lateral.
collateral.g: Parallel, in the same vein, side by side.

collect.e: From Middle English collecten, a borrowing from Old French collecter, from Medieval Latin collectare (“to collect money”).
From Middle English collecte, from Ecclesiastical Latin collēcta (“assembly; collect”), originally designating the gathering at the beginning of a liturgical celebration.
collect.g: The prayer said before the reading of the epistle lesson, especially one found in a prayerbook, as with the Book of Common Prayer.

collection.e: From Middle English colleccioun, collection, from Old French collection, from Latin collēctiō, collēctiōnem, from collēctus, from colligō (“collect together”), composed of con- + legō (“bring together, gather, collect”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- (“to gather, collect”). Equivalent to collect + -ion.
collection.g: A set of items or amount of material procured, gathered or presented together.

collector.e: From Middle English collectour, from Anglo-Norman collectour, from Late Latin collēctor, from Latin colligō (“to gather together”).
collector.g: A person who or thing that collects, or which creates or manages a collection.

college.e: From Middle English college, from Middle French college, from Old French college, from Latin collēgium.

collop.e: Late Middle English, of North Germanic origin, from Swedish kalops (“stewed meat”), from Old Swedish kollops (“slices of beef stew”).

colonnade.g: A series of columns at regular intervals.

colony.e: From Middle English colane, colonye, from Latin colōnia (“colony”), from colōnus (“farmer; colonist”), from colō (“till, cultivate, worship”), from earlier *quelō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to move; to turn (around)”).
colony.g: A geographical area under the remote control of a country; especially to extract resources or exploit labor from that area.

color.e: From Middle English colour, color, borrowed from Anglo-Norman colur, from Old French colour, color, from Latin color. Largely displaced English blee, Middle English blee (“color”), from Old English blēo.
color.g: The spectral composition of visible light.

colt.e: From Middle English colt, from Old English colt, from Proto-Germanic *kultaz (“plump; stump; thick shape, bulb”), from Proto-Indo-European *gelt- (“something round, pregnant belly, child in the womb”), from *gel- (“to ball up, amass”).
colt.g: A young male horse or similar young male equine, especially just after birth or less than a year old.

column.e: From Middle English columne, columpne, columpe, borrowed from Old French columne, from Latin columna (“a column, pillar, post”), originally a collateral form of columen, contraction culmen (“a pillar, top, crown, summit”).
column.g: A solid upright structure designed usually to support a larger structure above it, such as a roof or horizontal beam, but sometimes for deco

comb.e: From Middle English comb, from Old English camb (“comb”), from Proto-West Germanic *kamb, from Proto-Germanic *kambaz (“comb”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos (“tooth”), a doublet of cam.

come.e: From Middle English comen, cumen, from Old English cuman, from Proto-West Germanic *kweman, from Proto-Germanic *kwemaną (“to come”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷémt (“to step; to arrive”), from *gʷem- (“to come, step”).
come.g: To move nearer to the point of perspective.

comeliness.g: Quality of being comely; beauty, attractiveness.

comely.e: From Middle English comli (“beautiful, handsome; of noble birth, bearing, or character; convenient, appropriate, fitting”), from Old English cȳmlīċ (“comely, beautiful, lovely”), from Proto-West Germanic *kūmijalīk (“comely, convenient”), from Proto-Germanic *kūmijalīkaz (“comely, convenient”), from *kūmijaz (“delicate, weak”) + *-līkaz.

From Middle English comli, cumly, cumeliche (“beautifully, handsomely; gracefully; splendidly; fittingly, properly; well”), from Old English cȳme (adjective) (see etymology 1) + Middle English -li (suffix forming adverbs).
comely.g: Synonym of comelily (“in a comely manner: in an attractive or pleasing manner; in a manner which meets accepted moral or social norms”).

comer.e: From Middle English comere, equivalent to come + -er.
comer.g: One in a race who is catching up to others and shows promise of winning.

comes.g: The answer to the theme, or dux, in a fugue.

comfort.e: From Middle English comfort, from Old French cunfort, confort, from the stem of Late Latin confortō. It replaced Old English frofor, Middle English frovre.
From Middle English comforten, from Old French conforter, from Late Latin confortō (“to strengthen greatly”), itself from Latin con- (“together”) + fortis (“strong”).
comfort.g: To relieve the distress or suffering of; to provide comfort to.

comfortable.e: From Middle English comfortable, from Old French confortable, from conforter. By surface analysis, comfort + -able.
comfortable.g: Providing physical comfort and ease; agreeable.

comforter.e: From Middle English comfortour et al, from Anglo-Norman confortour, from Old French conforter.
comforter.g: A person who comforts someone who is suffering.

comfortless.e: From Middle English comfortles; equivalent to comfort + -less.
comfortless.g: Of a person: deprived of comfort; uncomforted.

coming.e: From Middle English cominge, comynge, comande, from Old English cumende, from Proto-Germanic *kwemandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *kwemaną (“to come”), equivalent to come + -ing (present participle ending).
coming.g: Used to express that one is on the way.

command.e: From Middle English commanden, commaunden, comaunden, comanden, from Old French comander, from Late Latin commandāre, from Latin commendāre. Ultimately from Latin com- + mandō (whence ultimately also commend (a doublet), mandate, and recommend), from manus + -dō.

commander.e: From Middle English comaundour, commaunder, comaunder, borrowed from Old French comandeor, cumandeur, from comander. By surface analysis, command + -er.
commander.g: One who exercises control and direction of a military or naval organization.

commandment.e: From Middle English comaundement, from Old French comandement, from comander.
commandment.g: A divinely ordained command, especially one of the Ten Commandments.

commemorate.e: Sporadic usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.
commemorate.g: To honour the memory of someone or something with a ceremony or object.

commend.e: From Middle English commenden, from Old French comender, from Latin commendō (“commend, entrust to, commit, recommend”), from com- + mandō (“to commit, intrust, enjoin”), from manus (“hand”) + dō (“to put”).

commendable.e: From Middle English commendable, from Middle French commendable, from Latin commendabilis, from commendare (“to commend, intrust to”), from com- + mandare (“to commit, intrust, enjoin”), from manus (“hand”) + dare (“to put”).
commendable.g: Worthy of commendation; deserving praise; admirable, creditable, or meritorious.

commendation.e: From Middle English commendacioun, from Old French commendacion (“approval, praise”), from Latin commendatio (“recommendation, commendation”), from commendare.
commendation.g: The act of commending; praise; favorable representation in words; recommendation.

commission.e: From Middle English commissioun, from Old French commission, from Latin commissiō (“sending together; commission”), from committō + -tiō (suffix forming nouns of action), from com- (“with”) + mittō (“to send”).
commission.g: A sending or mission (to do or accomplish something).

commissioner.e: From Middle English commissioner, from Anglo-Norman commissionaire, from Medieval Latin commissiōnārius. By surface analysis, commission + -er.

commit.e: From Middle English committen, itself borrowed from Latin committō (“to bring together, join, compare, commit (a wrong), incur, give in charge, etc.”), from com- (“together”) + mittō (“to send”).
commit.g: To give in trust; to put into charge or keeping; to entrust; to consign; used with to or formerly unto.

commitment.g: The act or an instance of committing, putting in charge, keeping, or trust, especially:

commodious.e: From Middle English commodious (“convenient, advantageous”), from Anglo-Norman commodious, Old French commodieux, directly from Medieval Latin commodiosus (“convenient, useful”), irregularly from Latin commodus (“suitable, fit, convenient”), from com- + modus (“measure, manner”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure”).
commodious.g: Spacious and convenient; roomy and comfortable.

common.e: From Middle English comun, from Anglo-Norman comun, from Old French comun (rare in the Gallo-Romance languages, but reinforced as a Carolingian calque of Proto-West Germanic *gamainī (“common”) in Old French), from Latin commūnis (“common, public, general”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱom-moy-ni-s (“held in common”).
common.g: Mutual; shared by more than one.

commonly.e: From Middle English comunly; equivalent to common + -ly.

commonwealth.e: From common (“public”) + wealth (“well-being”). From c. 1450 as common wele (commonweal). In the form common-wealth (common welthe) from c. 1520, used by Tyndale in the sense "secular society" in particular, for which other authors preferred publike weal.

commotion.e: From Middle French commocion, from Latin commōtiōnem, accusative singular of commōtiō, from commoveō + -tiō.

commune.e: From Middle English commune, comune, from Old French comune, commune, from Medieval Latin commūnia, from Latin commūne (“community, state”), from commūnis (“common”).
commune.g: A small community, often rural, whose members share in the ownership of property, and in the division of labour; the members of such a commu

commune.e: From Middle English communen, comunen, from Old French comuner (formed from comun (“common”)) and comunier (“to share”) (from Latin commūnico).
commune.g: To converse together with sympathy and confidence; to interchange sentiments or feelings; to take counsel.

communicate.e: Adapted borrowing of Latin commūnicāt- (past participial stem of commūnicō (“share, impart; make common”)) + -ate (verb-forming suffix), from commūnis (“common”) + -icō.
From Middle English communicate, an adapted borrowing of Latin commūnicātus (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), perfect passive participle of commūnicō (“to make commune”).

communication.e: From Middle English comunicacioun, communicacion (“discussion, association”), from Old French communicacion, from Latin commūnicātiōnem, accusative singular of commūnicātiō (“imparting, communicating”), from commūnicō (“to share, to impart”). Morphologically communicate + -ion.
communication.g: The act or fact of communicating anything; transmission.

communion.e: From Middle English comunioun, communyoun, from Anglo-Norman comunion or Middle French communion, from Ecclesiastical Latin commūniō (“communion”), from Latin commūnis.
communion.g: A joining together of minds or spirits; a mental connection.

community.e: From Late Middle English communite, borrowed from Old French communité, comunité, comunete (modern French communauté), from Classical Latin commūnitās (“community; public spirit”), from commūn(is) (“common, ordinary; of or for the community, public”) + -itās. By surface analysis, commun(e) + -ity.
community.g: A group sharing common characteristics, such as the same language, law, religion, or tradition.

compact.e: From Middle French compact, from Latin compāctus, perfect passive participle of compingō (“join together”), from com- (“together”) + pangō (“fasten”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ- (“to attach, fix, fasten”).
compact.g: Closely packed or densely constituted; having much material in a small volume.

companion.e: From Middle English companion, from Old French compaignon (“companion”) (modern French compagnon), from Late Latin compāniōn- (nominative singular compāniō, whence French copain).
companion.g: A friend, acquaintance or partner; someone with whom one spends time or accompanies

company.e: From Middle English companye (“a team; companionship”), from Old French compaignie (“companionship”) (Modern French: compagnie), possibly from Late Latin *compania, but this word is not attested. Old French compaignie is equivalent to Old French compaignon (Modern French: compagnon) + -ie.
company.g: A team; a group of people who work together for a common purpose.

comparable.e: From Middle English comparable, from Middle French comparable, from Latin comparābilis. By surface analysis, compare + -able.

compare.e: From Middle English comparen, from Old French comparer, from Latin comparare (“to prepare, procure”), from compar (“like or equal to another”), from com- + par (“equal”).
compare.g: To assess the similarities and differences between two or more things ["to compare X with Y"]. Having made the comparison of X with Y, one m

comparison.e: From Middle English comparisoun, borrowed from Old French comparison, a learned borrowing from Latin comparātiōnem.
comparison.g: The act of comparing or the state or process of being compared.

compass.e: From Middle English compas (“a circle, circuit, limit, form, a mathematical instrument”), from Old French compas, from Medieval Latin compassus (“a circle, a circuit”), from Latin com- (“together”) + passus (“a pace, step, later a pass, way, route”); see pass, pace.
compass.g: A magnetic or electronic device used to determine the cardinal directions (usually magnetic or true north).

compass.e: From Middle English compassen (“to go around, make a circuit, draw a circle, contrive, intend”), from Old French compasser; from the noun; see compass as a noun.
compass.g: To surround; to encircle; to environ; to stretch round.

compassing.e: From Middle English compassynge; equivalent to compass + -ing.

compassion.e: From Middle English compassioun, compassion, from Old French compassion, from Ecclesiastical Latin compassio (“sympathy”), from Latin compati, past participle compassus (“to suffer together with”), from com- (“together”) + pati (“to suffer”); see passion. By surface analysis, com- + passion.
compassion.g: Deep awareness of the suffering of others that people have to the point of them being motivated to relieve such states.

compassionate.e: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from a pseudo-Latin form of French compassionné, past participle of compassionner (“to feel sorry for”). By surface analysis, compassion + -ate.
compassionate.g: Having, feeling or showing compassion (to or toward someone).

compel.e: From Middle English compellen, borrowed from Middle French compellir, from Latin compellere, itself from com- (“together”) + pellere (“to drive”).

compensate.e: Borrowed from Latin compēnsātus, perfect passive participle of compensō (“to weight together one thing against another, balance, make good”), -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more.
compensate.g: To do (something good) after (something bad) happens.

compensation.e: From Middle English compensacioun, from Old French compensacion, from Latin compensātiōnem, accusative singular of compensātiō. Equivalent to compensate + -ion.
compensation.g: The act or principle of compensating.

compete.e: Borrowed from Middle French competer, from Latin competere (“to coincide, to be equal to, to be capable of”), from com- (“with”) + petō (“to seek; to aim for, strive for”).
compete.g: To be in battle or in a rivalry with another for the same thing, position, or reward; to contend.

competence.e: Borrowed from Middle French compétence, from Late Latin competentia.
competence.g: The quality or state of being competent, i.e. able or suitable for a general role.

competent.e: From Middle English competent, conpetent, from Old French competent (modern French compétent), from Latin competens, competentem, present participle of competō (“coincide, be equal to, be capable of”).
competent.g: Having sufficient skill, knowledge, ability, or qualifications.

competitor.e: Borrowed from Middle French compétiteur, from Latin competitor.
competitor.g: A person or organization against whom one is competing.

complacency.e: Late Middle English complacence, from Late Latin complacentia.
complacency.g: A feeling of contented self-satisfaction, especially when unaware of upcoming trouble.

complacent.e: Borrowed from Latin complacēns (“very pleasing”), present participle of complacēre (“to please at the same time, be very pleasing”), from com- (“together”) + placēre (“to please”); see please and compare complaisant.
complacent.g: Uncritically satisfied with oneself or one's achievements; smug.

complain.e: From Middle English complaynen, from Old French complaindre, from Medieval Latin complangere (“to bewail, complain”), from Latin com- (“together”) + plangere (“to strike, beat, as the breast in extreme grief, bewail”); see plain, plaint.
complain.g: To express feelings of pain, dissatisfaction, or resentment.

complaint.e: From Middle English compleynte, from Anglo-Norman compleint, from Old French compleindre, eventually from Latin planctus (whence plaint).

complete.e: From Middle English compleet (“full, complete”), borrowed from Old French complet or Latin completus, past participle of compleō (“to fill up, to complete”) (whence also complement, compliment), from com- + pleō (“to fill, to fulfill”) (whence also deplete, replete, plenty), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- (“to fill”) (English full).
complete.g: To finish; to make done; to reach the end.

completion.e: Borrowed from Latin completio. By surface analysis, complete + -tion.
completion.g: The act or state of being or making something complete; conclusion, accomplishment.

comply.e: From Italian complire, Catalan complir (“to complete, fulfil; to carry out”), Spanish cumplir (“to complete, fulfil”), (alternatively from Old French compli), from Latin complēre, from compleō (“to finish, complete; to fulfil”), from com- (prefix indicating completeness of an act) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm (“beside, near.
comply.g: To yield assent; to accord; to acquiesce, agree, consent; to adapt oneself, to conform.

component.e: Borrowed from Latin compōnēns, compōnēntis, present participle of compōnō (“assemble, put together”).
component.g: A smaller, self-contained part of a larger entity. Often refers to a manufactured object that is part of a larger device.

compose.e: From Middle English composen, from Old French composer (“to compose, compound, adjust, settle”), from com- + poser, as an adaptation of Latin componere (“to put together, compose”), from com- (“together”) + ponere (“to put, place”).
compose.g: To make something by merging parts.

composition.e: From Middle English composicioun, borrowed from Old French composicion, from Latin compositiō, compositiōnem.
composition.g: The act of putting together; assembly.

compound.e: Possibly from Malay kampong, kampung (“group of buildings, village”), via Dutch or Portuguese, altered under the influence of Etymology 2.
compound.g: An enclosure within which workers, prisoners, or soldiers are confined.

compound.e: From Middle English compounen, from Middle French componre, compondre (“to put together”), from Latin componō, from Latin com- (“together”) + ponō (“to put”).

comprehend.e: From Middle English comprehenden, from Latin comprehendere (“to grasp”), from the prefix com- + prehendere (“to seize”).
comprehend.g: To understand or grasp fully and thoroughly; to plumb.

comprehension.e: Borrowed from Middle French compréhension, from Latin comprehēnsiō (“taking together”), from com- (“with, together”) + prehendō (“take”).

compulsion.e: Borrowed from Middle French compulsion, from Late Latin compulsiō, from Latin compellere (“to compel, coerce”); see compel.
compulsion.g: An irrational need or irresistible urge to perform some action, often despite negative consequences.

conceal.e: From Middle English concelen, from Old French conceler (“hide, disguise”), from Latin concēlō, concēlāre (“carefully disguise”).
conceal.g: To hide something from view or from public knowledge, to try to keep something secret.

concede.e: From Middle English, from Old French conceder, from Latin concēdō (“give way, yield”), from con- (“wholly”) + cēdō (“to yield, give way, to go, grant”), from Proto-Indo-European *ked- (“to go, yield”).
concede.g: To yield or suffer; to surrender; to grant

conceit.e: From Middle English conceyte, formed from conceyven by analogy with pairs such as (Modern English) deceive~deceit, receive~receipt etc.
conceit.g: Something conceived in the mind; an idea, a thought.

conceive.e: From Middle English conceyven, from Old French concevoir, conceveir, from Latin concipiō, concipere (“to devise, to conceive”).
conceive.g: To have a child; to become pregnant (with).

conception.e: From Middle English concepcioun, borrowed from Old French conception, from Latin conceptiō (“a comprehending, a collection, composition, an expression, also a becoming pregnant”), from concipiō, past participle conceptus (“conceive”); see conceive. Equivalent to conceive + -tion.

concern.e: Borrowed from Middle French concerner, from Medieval Latin concernō, concernere (“I distinguish, have respect to”), from Latin concernō (“to mix, sift, or mingle together, as in a sieve”), combined form of con- + cernō (“distinguish”).
concern.g: That which affects one’s welfare or happiness. A matter of interest to someone.

concerning.e: From concern + -ing. The adjective and preposition follow from the verb.

concession.e: From late Middle English concession, from Middle French concession, from Latin concessiō (“a grant, permission, conceding”), from concēdō.

concision.e: Borrowed from French concision, from Latin concisiō(n).

conclude.e: From Middle English concluden, borrowed from Latin conclūdere (“to shut up, close, end”).
conclude.g: To end; to come to an end.

conclusion.e: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French conclusion, from Latin conclūsiō, from the past participle stem of conclūdere (“to conclude”), from con- + claudō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂u- (“key, hook, nail”). By surface analysis, conclude + -sion.
conclusion.g: The end, finish, close or last part of something.

concord.e: From French concorde, Latin concordia, from concors (“of the same mind, agreeing”); con- + cor, cordis (“heart”).
concord.g: A state of agreement; harmony; union.

concord.e: After Concord, Massachusetts, where the variety was developed.
concord.g: A variety of sweet American grape, with large dark blue (almost black) grapes in compact clusters; a Concord grape.

concourse.e: From Middle English concours, from Middle French concours and its etymon Latin concursus, concursum, from concurrere (“to run together”).
concourse.g: A large open space in or in front of a building where people can gather, particularly one joining various paths, as in a rail station or air

concubine.e: From Middle English concubine (first attested 1250–1300), from Anglo-Norman concubine, from Latin concubīna, equivalent to concub- (variant stem of concumbō (“to lie together”)) + feminine suffix -īna.
concubine.g: A sexual partner, especially a woman, to whom one is not or cannot be married.

concupiscence.e: From Latin concupīscentia, from concupīscō (“to desire strongly, to desire eagerly; to covet”).
concupiscence.g: An ardent desire, especially sexual desire; lust.

concur.e: Borrowed from Latin concurro (“to run together, agree”).
concur.g: To agree (in action or opinion); to have a common opinion; to coincide; to correspond.

condemn.e: From Middle English condempnen, from Old French condamner, from Latin condemnāre (“to sentence, condemn, blame”), from com- + damnāre (“to harm, condemn, damn”), from damnum (“damage, injury, loss”).
condemn.g: To strongly criticise or denounce; to excoriate.

condemnation.e: From Middle English condempnacioun, from Latin condemnātiō, condemnātiōnem.
condemnation.g: The act of condemning or pronouncing to be wrong.

condescend.e: From Middle English condescenden, condescendre (“to deign, condescend; to accede graciously; to agree; to agree to, give consent; to make a concession, yield; etc.”), from Old French condescendre (“to descend, go down; to agree or assent to”) (modern French condescendre).
condescend.g: To come down or go down; to descend.

condition.e: From Middle English condicioun, from Old French condicion (French condition), from Latin condicio. An unetymological change in spelling due to a confusion with conditio.

conduct.e: From Late Latin conductus (“defense, escort”), from Latin conductus, perfect passive participle of condūcō (“bring together”); see also conduce.
conduct.g: The act or method of controlling or directing.

conduit.e: From Middle English conduyt, condit, from Old French conduit, from Latin conductus.
conduit.g: A channel or pathway through which something is conducted, carried, etc.

confection.e: From Middle English confescioun, borrowed from Old French confeccion (French confection), borrowed from Latin cōnfectiōnem, from cōnfectus, past participle of cōnficiō (“prepare”), from con- (“with”) + faciō (“to make, do”). By surface analysis, confect + -ion. Originally "the making by means of ingredients".
confection.g: A food item prepared very sweet, frequently decorated in fine detail, and often preserved with sugar, such as a candy, sweetmeat, fruit pres

confectionary.e: From Late Latin cōnfectiōnārius (“one who prepares things by means of ingredients”), from Latin cōnfectiō (“preparing, producing”). By surface analysis, confection + -ary.
confectionary.g: Relating to, or of the nature of confections or their production.

confederacy.e: From Middle English confederacie, from Anglo-Norman confederacie, from Latin cōnfoederātiō.

confederate.e: Regular participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English. By surface analysis, con- + federate.
confederate.g: Of, relating to, or united in a confederacy

confer.e: From Early Modern English conferre, from Middle French conférer, from Old French conferer, from Latin cōnferō.
confer.g: To grant as a possession; to bestow.

conference.e: From Middle French conférence, from Medieval Latin cōnferentia, from Latin cōnferēns, omitting several steps, from con- + ferō.
conference.g: The act of consulting together formally; serious conversation or discussion; interchange of views.

confess.e: From Middle English confessen, from Anglo-Norman confesser, from Old French confesser, from Latin confessus (Old French confés), past participle of cōnfiteor (“to confess, admit”) from con- + fateor (“to admit”). Sense 6 is a semantic loan from Japanese 告(こく)白(はく) (kokuhaku).
confess.g: To admit to the truth, particularly in the context of sins or crimes committed.

confession.e: From Middle English confessioun, from Old French confession, from Latin cōnfessiō, cōnfessiōnem (“confession, acknowledgment, creed or avowal of one's faith”). Morphologically confess + -ion. Sense 6 is a calque of 告白 (kokuhaku).
confession.g: The open admittance of having done something (especially something bad).

confide.e: From Middle Scots confide, confyde (“to put trust in”), from Latin confīdere (“to put trust in, have confidence in”), from con- (“together”) + fidēre (“to trust”).

confidence.e: From Middle English confidence, from Latin cōnfīdentia (possibly via Old French confidence), from cōnfīdō (“believe, confide in”) from con- (“with”) + fīdō (“trust”). By surface analysis, confide + ence.

confident.e: From Middle French confident, from Latin confidens (“confident, i.e. self-confident, in a good or bad sense, bold, daring, audacious, impudent”), present participle of confidere (“to trust fully, confide”).

confine.e: From Middle French confiner, from confins, from Medieval Latin confines, from Latin confinium, from confīnis.
confine.g: To have a common boundary with; to border on.

confirm.e: From Middle English confirmen, confermen, from Old French confermer, from Latin cōnfirmāre (“to make firm, strengthen, establish”), from con- (“together”) + firmāre (“to make firm”), from firmus (“firm”).
confirm.g: To strengthen; to make firm or resolute.

confirmation.e: From Middle English confirmacioun, from Old French confirmacion, from Latin cōnfirmātiō, noun of process from cōnfirmātus (“confirmed”), perfect passive participle of cōnfirmāre, from con- (“with”) + firmāre (“to firm or strengthen”). Morphologically confirm + -ation.
confirmation.g: An official indicator that things will happen as planned.

confiscation.e: From Latin cōnfiscātiō. By surface analysis, confiscate + -ion.
confiscation.g: The act or process of confiscating.

conflict.e: From Latin cōnflīctus, from com- + flīctus, past participle of conflīgō (“to strike together”), from com- + flīgō (“strike”) (whence con-).
conflict.g: A clash or disagreement, often violent, between two or more opposing groups or individuals.

conform.e: From Middle English conformen, borrowed from Middle French and Anglo-Norman conformer, from Latin conformāre (“to mould, to shape after”).
conform.g: To adapt to something by more closely matching it, especially something normative.

conformable.g: Having the same shape or form; very similar.

conformity.e: From Middle English conformyte, from Middle French conformité. By surface analysis, conform + -ity.
conformity.g: The state of things being similar or identical.

confound.e: From Middle English confounden (“destroy, ruin, perplex”), from Anglo-Norman cunfundre and Old French confondre, from Latin cōnfundō (“to mingle, mix together”).

confront.e: From Middle French confronter, borrowed from Medieval Latin cōnfrontāre, from con- + frontem (“front, forehead”).
confront.g: To stand or meet facing, especially in competition, hostility or defiance; to come face to face with.

confuse.e: Back-formation from confused, from Middle English confused (“frustrated, ruined”), from Anglo-Norman confus, from Latin cōnfūsus, past participle of cōnfundō.
confuse.g: To puzzle, perplex, baffle, bewilder (somebody); to afflict by being complicated, contradictory, or otherwise difficult to understand.

confuse.e: From Middle English confus, from Old French confus, from Latin cōnfūsus, past participle of cōnfundō.

confused.e: Originally from Middle English confused (“frustrated, ruined”), from Anglo-Norman confus + Middle English -ed (past participial suffix), from Latin cōnfūsus, past participle of cōnfundō; now equivalent to confuse (a back-formation) + -ed.
confused.g: unable to think clearly or understand

confusion.e: From Middle English confusioun, from Old French confusion, from Latin confusio, confusionem. Morphologically confuse + -ion.
confusion.g: A lack of clarity or order.

congeal.e: From Middle English congelen, from Middle French congeler, from Latin congelare, cognate with Portuguese and Spanish congelar.
congeal.g: To change from a liquid to solid state, perhaps due to cold; called to freeze in nontechnical usage.

congratulate.g: To express one’s sympathetic pleasure or joy to the person(s) it is felt for

congregation.e: From Middle English congregacioun, from Old French congregacion, from Latin congregātiō, itself from congregō (“to herd into a flock”).
congregation.g: The act of congregating or collecting together.

conjurer.e: From Middle English conjurer, from Anglo-Norman conjurour (“conjurer, conspirator”). Equivalent to conjure + -er.

connect.e: From Latin connectere (“fasten together”), from con- (“together”) + nectere (“bind”), which is cognate with English knot and English knit.
connect.g: To join (to another object): to attach, or to be intended to attach or capable of attaching, to another object.

connection.e: From Middle English conneccioun, connexioun, conneccyon, conneccion, from Latin connexionem (nominative connexio (“a conclusion, binding together”)), from connectō, an alternative spelling of cōnectō (“to bind together”), from compound of co- (“together”) and nectō (“to bind”).

conquer.e: From Middle English conqueren, from Old French conquerre, from Late Latin conquaerere (“to knock, strike; to search for, procure”), from Latin con- + quaerere (“to seek, acquire”).
conquer.g: To defeat in combat; to subjugate.

conqueror.e: From Middle English conquerour, from Old French conquereor, from conquerre. By surface analysis, conquer + -or.

conscience.e: From Middle English conscience, from Old French conscience, from Latin conscientia (“knowledge within oneself”) (a calque of Ancient Greek σῠνείδησῐς (sŭneídēsĭs)), from consciens, present participle of conscire (“to know, to be conscious (of wrong)”), from com- (“together”) + scire (“to know”).
conscience.g: The ethical or moral sense of right and wrong, chiefly as it affects a person’s own behaviour and forms their attitude to their past actions

conscious.e: From Latin cōnscius (“conscious, conscious of guilt”), itself from con- (a form of com- (“together”)) + scīre (“to know”) + -us.
conscious.g: Alert, awake; with one's mental faculties active.

conscript.e: From Latin cōnscriptus, perfect passive participle of cōnscrībō (“write together; enroll”).
conscript.g: One who is compulsorily enrolled, often into a military service; a draftee.
A constructed script or writing system, especially for use with a conlang or spelling reform.

consecrate.e: Regular participial usage up until Early Modern English.

consecration.g: The act or ceremony of consecrating; the state of being consecrated; dedication.

consent.e: Recorded in Middle English since circa 1225, borrowed from Old French consentir, from Latin cōnsentīre (“to agree; to assent, consent”), itself from com- (“with”) + sentiō (“to feel”) (whence con-).
consent.g: To express willingness, to give permission.

consequence.e: From Middle English consequence, from Old French consequence, from Latin consequentia. While analysable as con- + sequence, its adjective form has a different origin.
consequence.g: An effect; something that follows a cause as a result.

consider.e: From Middle English consideren, from Middle French considerer, from Latin considerare.

consideration.e: From Middle English consideracioun, from Old French consideracion, from Latin cōnsīderātiō. By surface analysis, consider + -ation.
consideration.g: The thought process of considering, of taking multiple or specified factors into account (with of being the main corresponding adposition).

consign.e: Borrowed from Middle French consigner or directly from Latin cōnsignō (“furnish with a seal”), from con- + signō (“mark, sign”).
consign.g: To transfer to the custody of, usually for sale, transport, or safekeeping.

consist.e: From Middle French consister, from Latin consistō (“stand together, stop, become hard or solid, agree with, continue, exist”), from com- (“together”) + sistō (“to cause to stand, stand”).

consist.g: A lineup or sequence of railroad carriages or cars, with or without a locomotive, that form a unit.

consistent.e: Borrowed from Latin cōnsistēntem, present participle of cōnsistō (“to agree with; to continue”), from con- (prefix indicating a being or bringing together of several objects) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm (“beside, by, near, with”)) + sistō (“to cause to stand; to place, set”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *stísteh₂ti (“to be standing up.
consistent.g: Of a regularly occurring, dependable nature.

consolation.e: From Old French consolacion (French consolatio), from Latin cōnsōlātiō, from the deponent verb cōnsōlor (“I console, encourage”) with the -tiō suffix, while cōnsōlor comprises the intensifying prefix con- with the deponent verb sōlor (“I comfort, console”). Equivalent to console + -ation.
consolation.g: The act or example of consoling; the condition of being consoled.

console.e: Borrowed from French console (“bracket”, noun), from consoler (“to console, to comfort”, verb). Sense of “bracket” either due to a bracket alleviating the load, or due to brackets being decorated with the Christian figure of a consolateur (“consoler”), itself perhaps a pun on the first sense (alleviating load).
console.g: A stand-alone cabinet designed to stand on the floor; especially, one integrated with home entertainment equipment, such as a TV or stereo s

console.e: Borrowed from French consoler, from Latin cōnsōlor (“to console, offer solace”), root from Proto-Indo-European *selh₂- (“mercy, comfort”) (whence also solace).
console.g: To comfort (someone) in a time of grief, disappointment, etc.

consort.e: Borrowed from Middle French, ultimately from Latin cōnsors. As “companion or partner”, via Middle English consorte.

conspicuous.e: From Latin conspicuus (“visible, striking”), from cōnspicere (“to notice”), from con- (“with, together”) + specere (“to look at”).

conspiracy.e: From Middle English conspiracie, from Anglo-Norman conspiracie, from Latin cōnspīrātiō. By surface analysis, conspire + -acy.
conspiracy.g: An agreement or arrangement between multiple parties to do something harmful, immoral or subversive; an instance of collusion.

conspirator.e: From Middle English conspyratour, from Anglo-Norman conspiratour. By surface analysis, conspire + -ator.
conspirator.g: One of a group that acts in harmony to do something unlawful and unethical; a person who is part of a conspiracy.

conspire.e: From Middle English conspiren, from Old French conspirer, from Latin conspirare, conspīrō, from con- (combining form of cum (“with”)) + spīrō (“breathe”).
conspire.g: To secretly plot or make plans together, often with the intention to bring bad or illegal results; to collude, to connive, to plot.

constant.e: From Middle English constant, from Old French constant, from Latin constantem, accusative of constans, from cōnstāre (“to stand firm”).
constant.g: Unchanged through time or space; permanent.

constantly.g: With steadfastness; with resolve; in loyalty, faithfully.

constellation.e: From Middle English constellacioun, constillacioun (“(astrology) position of the moon or a planet in relation to the ascendant sign of the zodiac; horoscope; (astronomy) formation of fixed stars, constellation.
constellation.g: An arbitrary formation of stars perceived as a figure (especially one from mythology) or pattern, or a division of the sky including it, esp

constituency.g: A district represented by one or more elected officials.

constrain.e: From Middle English constreinen, from Old French constreindre, from Latin cōnstringō, from cōn- (“with, together”) + stringō (“to draw, bind or tie tight”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *streyg- (“to stroke, to shear, stiff”).
constrain.g: To force physically, by strong persuasion or pressuring; to compel; to oblige.

constraint.e: From Middle English constreynt, constreynte, from Old French constreinte, past participle of constreindre (“to constrain”), from Latin cōnstringō (corresponding to the past participle cōnstrictus).

construct.e: Borrowed from Latin cōnstrūctus, from cōnstruō (“to heap together”), from com- (“together”) + struō (“to heap up, pile”).

construction.e: From Middle English construccioun, construction, from Old French construction, from Latin cōnstructiō, from cōnstruere. Morphologically construct + -ion.

consult.e: From Middle French consulter, from Latin cōnsultum, from cōnsultus, from cōnsulō.
consult.g: A visit to consult somebody, such as a doctor; a consultation.

consultation.e: From Middle French consultation, from Latin consultatio. Morphologically consult + -ation.

consume.e: From Middle English consumen, from Old French consumer, from Latin cōnsūmere, cōnsūmō, from con- (“with, together”) + sūmō (“take; consume”), from sub- + emō (“to buy, take”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁em- (“to take, distribute”), possibly related to the root *nem- (“to take or give one's due”).

consummation.g: The act of consummating, or the state of being consummated; the state of being completed; completion.

consumption.e: From con- + Latin sūmptus + -ion, from Middle English consumpcioun, from Old French consumpcion, from Latin cōnsūmptiō, from cōnsūmō + -tiō, from con- (“with, together”) + sūmō (“take; consume”). Equivalent to consume + -tion.
consumption.g: The act of eating, drinking or using.

contact.e: From Latin contactus, from contingō (“to touch on all sides”), from tangō (“to touch”). Used in English since the 17th century.
contact.g: The act of touching physically; being in close association.

contain.e: From Middle English conteinen, borrowed from Old French contenir, from Latin continēre (“to hold or keep together, comprise, contain”), combined form of con- (“together”) + teneō (“to hold”).

container.e: From Middle English conteiner, equivalent to contain + -er.
container.g: Someone who contains; something that contains.

contaminate.e: Participial usage up until Early Modern English.

contamination.g: The act or process of contaminating.

contemn.e: From Middle English contempnen, from Old French contemner, from Latin contemnō (“to scorn”).
contemn.g: To disdain; to value at little or nothing; to treat or regard with contempt.

contemporary.e: From Medieval Latin contemporārius, from Latin con- (“with, together”) + temporārius, an adjective derived from tempus (“time”).
contemporary.g: From the same time period, coexistent in time; contemporaneous.

contempt.e: From Latin contemptus (“scorn”), from contemnō (“to scorn, despise”), from com- + temnō (“to despise”).
contempt.g: The state or act of contemning; the feeling or attitude of regarding someone or something as inferior, base, or worthless; scorn, disdain.

contemptible.e: From Middle English contemptible, from Latin contemptibilis. By surface analysis, contempt + -ible.

contemptuous.g: Showing contempt; expressing disdain; showing a lack of respect.

contend.e: From Middle English contenden, borrowed from Old French contendre, from Latin contendere (“to stretch out, extend, strive after, contend”), from com- (“together”) + tendere (“to stretch”); see tend, and compare attend, extend, intend, subtend.
contend.g: To be in opposition; to contest; to dispute; to vie; to quarrel; to fight.

content.e: From Middle English contenten (“to satisfy”), from Latin contentus (“contained; satisfied”), past participle of continēre (“to contain”).

From Middle English content (plural contentes, contence), from Latin contentus, past participle of continēre (“to hold in, contain”), as Etymology 1, above. English apparently developed a substantive form of the adjective, which is not mirrored in Romance languages.

contention.e: From Middle English contencion, borrowed from Old French contencion, from Latin contentio, contentionem, from contendō (past participle contentus); equivalent to contend + -tion (similar formation to attention).

contentious.e: From Middle French contentieux, from Latin contentiōsus (“quarrelsome, perverse”), from contentiō (“contention”), from contendere, past participle contentus (“to contend”). Equivalent to English contention + -ous.
contentious.g: Marked by heated arguments or controversy.

contentment.e: From Middle French contentement. By surface analysis, content + -ment.
contentment.g: The state or degree of being contented or satisfied.

contest.e: From French contester, from Old French, from Latin contestor (“to call to witness”).

context.g: The surroundings, circumstances, environment, background or settings that determine, specify, or clarify the meaning of an event or other oc

continual.e: From Middle English continuel, from Old French continuel, formed from Latin continuus (“continuous”) with the suffix -el, equivalent to continue + -al.

continuance.e: From Middle English continuance, contynuaunce, from Old French continuance, from continuer.

continue.e: From Middle English continuen, from Old French continuer, from Latin continuō.
continue.g: To proceed with (doing an activity); to prolong (an activity).

contort.e: Equivalent to con- + -tort; from Middle English, borrowed from Latin contortus, past participle of contorqueō, from com- + torqueō (“twist, turn”).
contort.g: To twist in a violent manner.

contract.e: From Middle English, from Old French contract, from Latin contractus (noun), from contrahere (“to bring together, to bring about, to conclude a bargain”) + -tus (suffix forming nouns from verbs).
contract.g: An agreement between two or more parties, to perform a specific job or work order, often temporary or of fixed duration and usually governed

contract.e: From Middle English, from Middle French contracter, from Latin contractum, past participle of contrahere (“to bring together, to bring about, to conclude a bargain”), from con- (“with, together”) + trahere (“to draw, to pull”). The verb developed after the noun, and originally meant only "draw together"; the sense "make a contract with" developed later.
contract.g: To draw together or nearer; to shorten, narrow, or lessen.

contradict.e: From Latin contrādictus (“contradicted”), the past participle of contrādīcō (“speak against”) (originally two words).
contradict.g: To deny the truth or validity of (a statement or statements).

contradiction.e: From Middle English contradiccioun, contradiction, from Old French contradiction, from Latin contrādictiō, from contrādīcō (“speak against”).

contrariwise.e: From Middle English contrary-wyse; equivalent to contrary + -wise.
contrariwise.g: In the contrary or opposite way, order, or direction.

contrary.e: From Middle English contrarie, compare French contraire, from Old French contraire, from Latin contrārius (“opposite, opposed, contrary”), from contrā (“against”).
contrary.g: Opposite; in an opposite direction; in opposition; adverse.

contribute.e: From Latin contribūtus, perfect passive participle of contribuō (“to bring together; to unite”), from con- (“together”) + tribuō (“to bestow”), from tribus (“tribe”), derived from trēs (“three”), from Proto-Italic *trēs, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.
contribute.g: To give something that is or becomes part of a larger whole.

contribution.e: From Middle English contribucioun, contribucion, from Old French contribution, from Latin contribūtiōnem, contribūtiō, from Latin contribuēre. By surface analysis, contribute + -ion.
contribution.g: Something given or offered that adds to a larger whole.

contrite.e: From Middle English contrit, from Old French contrit, from Latin contrītus (literally “ground to pieces”), perfect passive participle of conterō (“grind, bruise”), from con- + terō (“rub, wear away”).
contrite.g: Sincerely penitent or feeling regret or sorrow, especially for one’s own actions.

contrive.e: From Middle English contrive (15th c.), an alteration of contreve(n), controve(n) (“to invent”, 14th c.), from Old French controver, derived from trover (“to find”). The Middle English form with -e- reflects the Old French tonic stem (il contrueve), but the shift to -i- seems to be unclear.
contrive.g: To invent by an exercise of ingeniosity; to devise

control.e: From Middle English controllen, from Old French contrerole, from Medieval Latin contrārotulus (“a counter-roll or register used to verify accounts”), from Latin contrā (“against, opposite”) + Medieval Latin rotulus, Latin rotula (“roll, a little wheel”), diminutive of rota (“a wheel”).
control.g: To exercise influence over; to suggest or dictate the behavior of.

controversy.e: From Middle English controversie, from Old French controversie, from Latin contrōversia (“debate, contention, controversy”), from contrōversus (“turned in an opposite direction”).
controversy.g: A debate or discussion of opposing opinions; (generally) strife.

convene.e: Borrowed from Middle French convenir, from Latin convenio, convenire (“come together”), from con- (“with, together”) + veniō (“come”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷm̥yéti, from the root *gʷem-.
convene.g: To come together; to meet; to unite.

convenient.e: From Middle English convenient, from Latin conveniēns (“fit, suitable, convenient”), present participle of conveniō, convinīre (“to come together, suit”); see convene and compare covenant.
convenient.g: Serving to reduce a difficulty, or accessible with minimum difficulty; expedient.

conversant.e: From Old French conversant, present participle of converser.
conversant.g: Closely familiar; current; having frequent interaction.

conversation.e: From Middle English conversacioun, from Old French conversacion and its etymon, Latin conversātiōnem, accusative singular of conversātiō (“conversation”), from conversor (“abide, keep company with”). Morphologically converse + -ation.
conversation.g: Expression and exchange of individual ideas through talking with other people; also, a set instance or occasion of such talking.

conversion.e: From Middle English conversion, conversioun, borrowed from Anglo-Norman conversion, from Latin conversiō, from convertō.
conversion.g: The act of converting something or someone.

convert.e: From Middle English converten, from Old French convertir, from Latin converto (“turn around”).
convert.g: To transform or change (something) into another form, substance, state, or product.

convey.e: From Middle English conveien, from Old French conveier (French convoyer), from Vulgar Latin *convio, from Classical Latin via (“way”).
convey.g: To move (something) from one place to another.

convict.e: From Middle English convicten, from Anglo-Norman convicter, from Latin convictus, the past participle of convincō (“to convict”).
convict.g: To find guilty, as a result of legal proceedings, or (informal) in a moral sense.

conviction.e: From late Middle English conviction, from Anglo-Norman conviction, from Latin convictiō, from convictus, the past participle of convincō (“to convict”). Equivalent to convict + -ion.

convince.e: Borrowed from Latin convincō (“to refute, prove”), from con- + vincō (“to conquer, vanquish”).
convince.g: To make someone believe, or feel sure about something, especially by using logic, argument or evidence.

convocation.e: From Middle English convocacioun, from Old French convocation, from Latin convocatio, convocationem.
convocation.g: The act of calling or assembling by summons.

convulse.e: From Latin convulsus, past participle of convellere (“to pluck up, dislocate, convulse”), from com- (“together”) + vellere (“to pluck, pull”).
convulse.g: To suffer violent involuntary contractions of the muscles, causing one's body to contort.

convulsion.g: An intense, paroxysmal, involuntary muscular contraction.

coo.g: The murmuring sound made by a dove or pigeon.

cook.e: From Middle English cook, from Old English cōc (“a cook”), from Latin cocus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pekʷ- (“to cook, become ripe”).

cooked.e: From the past tense of the verb cook.

cooking.e: From cook + -ing. The noun and adjective follow from the verb. The use of the word cooking to describe cheap bitter was popularized by the title character of the BBC sitcom Oh No, It’s Selwyn Froggitt (1974-1978). It refers to cooking sherry, a kind of sherry used in cooking but not suitable for drinking on its own.
cooking.g: The process of preparing food by using heat.

cool.e: From Middle English cool, from Old English cōl (“cool, cold, tranquil, calm”), from Proto-West Germanic *kōl(ī), from Proto-Germanic *kōluz (“cool”), from *kalaną (“to be cold, to freeze”), Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to be cold, to freeze”).

cool.g: A measure of butter, usually around 40lb; a container holding such an amount of butter.

coolness.e: From Middle English colnes, colnesse, from Old English cōlnes, cœ̄lnes, cēlnes (“coolness; cool air, breeze”), from Proto-West Germanic *kōlinassī, equivalent to cool + -ness.

coordinate.e: From Medieval Latin coōrdinātus, perfect passive participle of coōrdinō (“arrange together”), from co- + ōrdinō, equivalent to co- + ordinate.
From a substantivation of the above adjective, see Etymology 1 and -ate (noun-forming suffix) for more.
coordinate.g: A number representing the position of a point along a line, arc, or similar one-dimensional figure.

coping.e: From cope + -ing. The sense referring to a brick wall is cope (sense 2), used in the sense "dress in a cope," "to cover."
coping.g: The top layer of a brick wall, especially one that slopes in order to throw off water.

copper.e: From cop (“ball of thread wound on to a spindle in a spinning machine”) + -er (suffix denoting things relating to the words to which the suffix is attached to).
copper.g: A component of the cop (“conical ball of thread wound on to the spindle”) in a spinning machine.

coppersmith.g: A person who forges things out of copper.

copulation.e: From Middle French copulation, from Latin copulo (“to join, unite, connect”).
copulation.g: The act of coupling or joining; union; conjunction.

copy.e: From Middle English copy, copie, from Old French copie (“abundance, plenty; transcript, copy”), from Medieval Latin copia (“reproduction, transcript”), from Latin cōpia (“plenty, abundance”), from *coopia, from co- (“together”) + ops (“wealth, riches”).
copy.g: The result of copying; an identical or nearly identical duplicate of an original.

copy.e: From Middle English copien, from Old French copier and Medieval Latin cōpiō.
copy.g: To produce an object identical to a given object.

cor.e: A minced oath or dialectal variant of God.

cor.g: Any of various former units of volume

coral.e: From Old French coral (French corail), from Latin corallium, from Ancient Greek κοράλλιον (korállion, “coral”). Probably ultimately of Semitic origin, compare Hebrew גּוֹרָל (goral, “small pebble”), Arabic جَرَل (jaral, “small stone”), originally referring to the red variety found in the Mediterranean.
coral.g: Any of many species of marine invertebrates in the class Anthozoa, most of which build hard calcium carbonate skeletons and form colonies, o

cord.e: From Middle English corde, from Old French corde, from Latin chorda, from Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ, “string of gut, the string of a lyre”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰerH- (“bowels, intestines”).
cord.g: A long, thin, flexible length of twisted yarns (strands) of fibre (a rope, for example).

coriander.e: From Middle English coriandre, from Anglo-Norman coriandre, from Old French corïandre, from Latin coriandrum, from Ancient Greek κορίανδρον (koríandron), of uncertain origin. Beekes supposes that cluster -dn- implies a Pre-Greek word, and hypothesizes that *koriaⁿdro- may have dissimilated to *koriaⁿdno-.
coriander.g: The annual herb Coriandrum sativum, used in many cuisines.

cormorant.e: From Middle English cormeraunt (“great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo); other types of aquatic bird”), from Old French cormaran, cor-maraunt (modern French cormoran), possibly variants of *corp-marin, from Medieval Latin corvus marīnus (literally “sea-raven”), with the ending -morant possibly derived from French moran (“marine, maritime”).
cormorant.g: Any of various medium-large black seabirds of the family Phalacrocoracidae which dive into water for fish and other aquatic animals, found t

corn.e: From Middle English corn, from Old English corn, from Proto-West Germanic *korn, from Proto-Germanic *kurną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm (“grain; worn-down”), from *ǵerh₂- (“grow old, mature”). The sense maize (Zea mays) is an ellipsis of Indian corn that developed in 18th century North America.
corn.g: Any cereal plant (or its grain) that is the main crop or staple of a country or region.

corn.e: English cornInherited from Middle English corne, from Old French corn (modern French cor), from Latin cornū.
corn.g: A type of callus, usually on the feet or hands.

corner.e: From Middle English corner, from Anglo-Norman cornere (compare Old French cornier, corniere (“corner”)), from Old French corne (“corner, angle”, literally “a horn, projecting point”), from Vulgar Latin *corna (“horn”), from Latin cornua, plural of cornū (“projecting point, end, horn”).
corner.g: The point where two converging lines meet; an angle, either external or internal.

corner.e: From corn + -er. Piecewise doublet of grainer.
corner.g: One who corns, or preserves food in salt.

cornerstone.e: From Middle English corner ston; equivalent to corner + stone. The figurative sense is in part after Psalm 118:22, and is also quoted several times in the New Testament.
cornerstone.g: A stone forming the base at the corner of a building.

cornet.e: From Middle English cornet, from Old French cornet, a diminutive of a popular reflex of Latin cornū (“horn”).
cornet.g: A musical instrument of the brass family, slightly smaller than a trumpet, usually in the musical key of B-flat.

cornet.e: From Middle French cornette, diminutive of corne, from Latin cornua (“horns”).
cornet.g: The white headdress worn by the Sisters of Charity.

corpse.e: From Middle English, from earlier corse, from Old French cors, from Latin corpus (“body”). The ⟨p⟩ was inserted due to the original Latin spelling. The verb sense derives from the notion of being unable to control laughter while acting as dead body.
corpse.g: A dead body, especially that of a human as opposed to an animal.

correct.e: Borrowed from French correct, from Latin correctus (“improved, amended, correct”), past participle of corrigere, conrigere (“to make straight, make right, make better, improve, correct”), from con- (“together”) + combining form of regō, regere (“I rule, make straight”).
From Middle English correcten, borrowed from Anglo-Norman correcter, from Latin correctus.
correct.g: To make something that was wrong become right; to remove error from.

correction.e: From Middle English correccioun, correction, from Old French correccion (French correction), from Latin corrēctiō.

correspond.e: From Middle French correspondre, from Latin com- (“with”) + respondeo (“to match, to answer to”), equivalent to co- + respond.
correspond.g: To be equivalent or similar in character, quantity, quality, origin, structure, function etc.

corresponding.g: A correspondence; the situation where things correspond or match.

corrode.e: From Middle English corrōden, that borrowed from Old French corroder or directly from Latin corrōdere (“to gnaw”), from con- (“completely”) + rōdere (“to gnaw”).
corrode.g: To eat away bit by bit; to wear away or diminish by gradually separating or destroying small particles of, as by action of a strong acid or

corrosion.e: From Middle English corrosioun, from Old French corrosion, or its source, Late Latin corrōsiōnem, accusative singular of corrōsiō (“gnawing away, corroding”), from Latin corrōdō (“gnaw away, corrode”).
corrosion.g: The act of corroding or the condition so produced.

corrupt.e: From Middle English corrupten, derived from Latin corruptus, past participle of corrumpō (“to destroy, ruin, injure, spoil, corrupt, bribe”), from com- (“together”) + rumpō (“to break in pieces”).
corrupt.g: Willing to act dishonestly for personal gain; accepting bribes.

corrupter.g: One who or that which corrupts.

corruptible.e: From Middle English corruptible, from Latin corruptibilis.

corruption.e: Borrowed from French corruption, from Latin corruptiō, equivalent to corrupt + -ion.
corruption.g: The act of corrupting or of impairing integrity, virtue, or moral principle; the state of being corrupted or debased; loss of purity or inte

cosmetics.e: From French cosmétique, from Ancient Greek κοσμητική (kosmētikḗ, “the art of dress and ornament”), from κοσμητικός (kosmētikós), an adjective of κοσμέω (kosméō, “to order, to arrange, to rule, to adorn, to equip, to dress, to embellish”).
cosmetics.g: Preparations applied externally to change or enhance the beauty of skin, hair, nails, lips, and eyes.

cost.e: From Middle English costen (verb), borrowed from Old French coster, from Medieval Latin cōstō, from Latin cōnstō, from Proto-Italic *komstaēō. By surface analysis, con- (“together”) + stō (“stand”).
cost.g: To incur a charge of; to require payment of a (specified) price.

cost.e: From Middle English cost, from Old English cost (“option, choice, possibility, manner, way, condition”), from Old Norse kostr (“choice, opportunity, chance, condition, state, quality”), from Proto-Germanic *kustuz (“choice, trial”) (or Proto-Germanic *kustiz (“choice, trial”)), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus (“to enjoy, taste”).
cost.g: Manner; way; means; available course; contrivance.

costly.e: From Middle English costly, costely, costeley, equivalent to cost + -ly.

cot.e: Borrowed from Hindi खाट (khāṭ), from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀔𑀝𑁆𑀝𑀸 (khaṭṭā), from Sanskrit खट्वा (khaṭvā, “bedstead”).
cot.g: A simple bed, especially one for portable or temporary purposes.

cot.e: From Middle English cot, cote, from Old English cot and cote (“cot, cottage”), from Proto-Germanic *kutą, *kutǭ (compare Old Norse kot, Middle High German kūz (“execution pit”)), from Scythian (compare Avestan 𐬐𐬀𐬙𐬀 (kata, “chamber”)).

cote.e: From Middle English cote, from the Old English cote, the feminine form of cot (“small house”); doublet of cot (in the sense of “cottage”) and more distantly related to cottage.
Probably related to French côté (“side”) via Middle French costé.
cote.g: To go side by side with; hence, to pass by; to outrun and get before.

cottage.e: Late Middle English, from Anglo-Norman cotage and Medieval Latin cotagium, from Old Northern French cot, cote (“cottage, hut”) + -age (“surrounding property”), from Old Norse kot.

couch.e: From Middle English couche, cowche, from Old French couche, from the verb (see below).
couch.g: An item of furniture, often upholstered, for the comfortable seating of more than one person; a sofa.

couch.e: From Middle English couchen, from Old French (se) couchier, (se) colchier (“go to bed, lay down”), from Latin collocāre (“set in place”), from com- (“together, with”) + locāre.
couch.g: To lie down; to recline (upon a couch or other place of repose).

couching.e: From Middle English couchynge; equivalent to couch + -ing.
couching.g: The act of one who couches.

coulter.e: From Middle English culter, from Old English culter, from Latin culter (“a knife”). For the phonetic development, see poultry.
coulter.g: A cutter, consisting of a blade in either knife form or disk form, attached to the ploughbeam of a plough to cut the sward, in front of the

council.e: From Middle English counseil (“meeting, conference, commune”), from Old French conseil (“advice, deliberation, thought”), from Latin cōnsilium (“plan, intention, design, purpose”), from cōnsulō (“consult, seek counsel from, take counsel from, deliberate, reflect”), from Proto-Indo-European *selh₁- (“take, grab”).
council.g: A committee that leads or governs (e.g. city council, student council).

counsel.e: From Middle English counseil, conseil, from Old French conseil, from Latin cōnsilium, of unknown origin but possibly from either com- + calō (via a phonetic variant of concilium) or cōnsulō.
counsel.g: The exchange of opinions and advice especially in legal issues; consultation.

counsel.e: From Middle English counseilen, from Old French conseiller, from Latin cōnsilior, from cōnsilium.
counsel.g: To give advice, especially professional advice, to (somebody).

counselor.e: From Middle English counseilour, counseiler, from Anglo-Norman cunseiler, from Old French conseillier, from Latin cōnsiliārius, agent noun from cōnsilior (“to take counsel”), from cōnsilium (“plan, council, wisdom, advice”).
counselor.g: A professional who counsels people, especially on personal problems.

count.e: From Middle English counten, borrowed from Anglo-Norman conter, from Old French conter (“add up; tell a story”), from Latin computō (“to compute”). In this sense, displaced native Old English tellan, whence Modern English tell.

From Middle English counte, from Anglo-Norman conte and Old French comte (“count”), from Latin comes (“companion”) (more specifically derived from its accusative form comitem) in the sense of "noble fighting alongside the king".
count.g: The male ruler of a county.

countenance.e: From Middle English contenaunce, countenaunce, from Anglo-Norman countenance and Old French contenance, from the present participle of contenir, or from Late Latin continentia, and therefore a doublet of continence.
countenance.g: Appearance, especially the features and expression of the face.

countervail.e: From Anglo-Norman countrevaloir (Old French contrevaloir), from Latin contrā valēre (“to be strong against”).
countervail.g: To have the same value or number as.

country.e: From Middle English contre, borrowed from Old French contree, from Vulgar Latin *(terra) contrāta (“facing land”), from Latin contrā (“against”) + -āta (noun-forming suffix). Unrelated to county. From around 1300 as "area surrounding a walled city or town.
country.g: The territory of a nation; a sovereign state or a region once independent and still distinct in institutions, language, etc.

couple.e: From Middle English couple, from Old French couple, from Latin cōpula.
couple.g: Two of the same kind connected or considered together.

coupling.e: From Middle English couplynge; equivalent to couple + -ing.
coupling.g: The act of joining together to form a couple.

courage.e: From Middle English corage, from Old French corage (French courage), from Vulgar Latin *corāticum, from Latin cor (“heart”). Distantly related to cardiac (“of the heart”), which is from Greek, but from the same Proto-Indo-European root.
courage.g: The quality of being confident, not afraid or easily intimidated, but without being incautious or inconsiderate.

courageous.e: From Middle English corajous, from Old French corageus, from corage + -eus.
courageous.g: Of a person, displaying or possessing courage.

courier.e: From a convergence of Middle English corour, currour, from Old French coreor, agent noun of corir (“to run”), and Middle English courier, a borrowing of Middle French courrier, from Italian corriere.

course.e: From Middle English cours, from Old French cours, from Latin cursus (“course of a race”), from currō (“run”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”).

court.e: From Middle English court, from Old French cort, curt, from Late Latin cōrs, contracted from Latin cohors. Professional tennis players playing on a tennis court (noun sense 5) in New Delhi, India.
court.g: An enclosed space; a courtyard; an uncovered area shut in by the walls of a building, or by different buildings; also, a space opening from

courteous.e: From Middle English curteis, from Old French curteis (French courtois), from cort (“court”). By surface analysis, court + -eous.
courteous.g: Showing regard or thought for others; especially, displaying good manners or etiquette.

courteously.e: From Middle English curteisly, curteisliche; equivalent to courteous + -ly.
courteously.g: In a courteous manner; with obliging civility or condescension; politely.

courtroom.g: The room where a judge presides over hearings and trials, sometimes with a jury.

courtyard.g: An area, open to the sky, partially or wholly surrounded by walls or buildings.

cousins.e: From cousin + -s (suffix forming pluralia tantum, regular plurals of nouns, and the third-person singular indicative present tense forms of verbs). The plural noun noun 1 sense 1 (“American or British intelligence services”) was popularized in the works of the English author John le Carré (David John Moore Cornwell; 1930–2020).
cousins.g: The American intelligence services (from a British perspective) or the British intelligence services (from an American perspective).

covenant.e: From Middle English covenaunt, borrowed from Old French covenant (“agreement”), from Latin conveniēns, convenientem (“agreeing, agreeable, suitable, convenient”), present participle of conveniō (“to agree”).
covenant.g: An agreement to do or not do a particular thing.

cover.e: From Middle English coveren, borrowed from Old French covrir, cueuvrir (modern French couvrir), from Late Latin coperire, from Latin cooperiō (“to cover completely”), from co- (intensive prefix) + operiō (“to close, cover”).

cover-up.g: An attempt to conceal or disguise something, especially a wrongdoing or a mistake.

covering.e: Present participle or participial adjective from cover (verb) + -ing; or, from Middle English coverynge, participle form of coveren, keveren (“to cover”).

covert.e: From Middle English covert, from Old French covert, past participle of covrir (“to cover”) (corresponding to Latin coopertus); cognate to cover. Not closely related to overt, despite what the most common pronunciation would suggest.

covertly.e: From Middle English covertli, equivalent to covert + -ly.

covet.e: From Middle English coveten, coveiten, coveyten, from Old French covoitier (modern French convoiter), from covoitié (“desire”), presumably modified from Latin cupiditas.
covet.g: To wish for with eagerness; to desire possession of, often enviously.

covetous.e: From Middle English coveitous, from Anglo-Norman *cuveitus, from Medieval Latin as if *cupiditosus, from Latin cupiditas (“desire”); see covet.
covetous.g: Distastefully desirous or keen, especially for something belonging to someone else; avaricious.

covetousness.e: From Middle English covatusnes, covetousnes, coveytousnesse; equivalent to covetous + -ness.
covetousness.g: Immoderate desire for the possession of something, especially for wealth.

cow.e: From Middle English cow, cou, from Old English cū (“cow”), from Proto-West Germanic *kō, from Proto-Germanic *kōz (“cow”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws (“cow”).
cow.g: An adult female of the species Bos taurus, especially one that has calved.

cow.e: Probably from Old Norse kúga (“to oppress”) (whence also Norwegian and Danish kue, Swedish kuva); compare Icelandic kúfa (“to set on top”) and Faroese kúga (“to oppress”).
cow.g: To intimidate; to daunt the spirits or courage of.

cowardly.e: From Middle English *cowardly (adjective) and cowardly (adverb), equivalent to coward + -ly.
cowardly.g: Showing cowardice; lacking in courage; weakly fearful.

cower.e: From Middle English couren, cowre, from Middle Low German kûren (“to lie in wait; linger”) or from North Germanic (Icelandic kúra (“to doze”)); according to Pokorny, all are ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to curve, bend”), see also Proto-Germanic *kuddô (“shell, pod”). Unrelated to coward, which is of Latin origin.
cower.g: To crouch or cringe, or to avoid or shy away from something, in fear.

can.e: From Middle English can, first and third person singular of connen, cunnen (“to be able, know how”), from Old English can(n), first and third person singular of cunnan (“to know how”), from Proto-West Germanic *kunnan, from Proto-Germanic *kunnaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (whence also know).
From Middle English canne, from Old English canne (“glass, container, cup, jar”), from Proto-Germanic *kannǭ (“can, tankard, mug, cup”).
can.g: A container or vessel, especially for liquids, usually made of metal.
